abstract:
Laminin-332 is a key extracellular matrix (ECM) protein that supports keratinocyte adhesion, migration and re-epithelialization during wound healing. Its loss, as in junctional epidermolysis bullosa, disrupts re-epithelialization, which highlights its therapeutic relevance. However, direct application of full-length laminin or its fragments is limited by poor stability and high production costs. As an alternative, biomaterial scaffolds are being developed. The capsular antigen F1 (Caf1) is one such scaffold, offering a stable, customizable platform for presenting bioactive motifs in a more practical format.
To develop stable Caf1 scaffolds displaying laminin-332 motifs and evaluate their therapeutic potential in promoting epithelial repair under healthy and laminin-deficient conditions, with the goal of enabling clinically translatable wound-healing strategies.
Laminin-332-derived peptide motifs were identified through a systematic literature review and ranked using a scoring system. Leading candidates were engineered into Caf1 and expressed in Escherichia coli. Keratinocyte migration, motility, adhesion and phospho-SMAD2 (pSMAD2) signalling were assessed in vitro using normal human epidermal keratinocytes and laminin subunit alpha-3 (LAMA3)-knockdown cells cultured on Caf1-coated plates. An ex vivo human skin wound model was used to assess translational relevance: wounded skin explants were treated with Caf1 constructs and cultured at the air-liquid interface for 7 days. Re-epithelialization and epithelial thickness were evaluated by haematoxylin and eosin staining.
Caf1 proteins displaying laminin-332-derived motifs were expressed in E. coli and purified. Among the engineered constructs, Caf1-J3 and Caf1-J4 significantly enhanced keratinocyte migration and single-cell motility in vitro. Combined application further accelerated wound closure, suggesting complementary effects. In LAMA3-deficient keratinocytes, these coatings restored adhesion, promoted actin cytoskeletal organization and reduced nuclear pSMAD2 levels. In ex vivo wounded human skin, they also promoted re-epithelialization and supported homogeneous neoepidermis formation.
These findings show that short laminin-332-derived motifs, when presented on the Caf1 scaffold, can mimic and partially recover key basement membrane functions in epithelial repair. Caf1-J3 and Caf1-J4 function as minimal bioactive units that restore keratinocyte cell adhesion and modulate key signalling pathways involved in wound healing. This modular protein platform offers a clinically relevant strategy for chronic wounds and ECM-deficient skin, and provides a foundation for next-generation regenerative therapies.

Type="plain-language-summary" Language="eng"><AbstractText>Wound healing is a vital process that restores the skin after an injury. In people with chronic wounds or with some inherited skin conditions this process can be severely impaired. One major cause of this is the loss of key structural proteins in the skin. One protein called ‘laminin-332’ helps some skin cells attach to the underlying tissue and move to close a wound. While laminin-332 is essential in wound healing, using it as a treatment is difficult. This is because it is very unstable and expensive. Bioengineering is the use of engineering principles to design and improve biological systems. We developed a new type of bioengineered material using a stable bacterial protein called Caf1. This is called a ‘Caf1 scaffold’. We attached short, functional segments from the laminin-332 protein to the Caf1 scaffold. We did this to create custom-designed materials that mimic natural skin support structures. These bioengineered materials were then tested in the lab on human skin cells and samples of wounded skin. We found that two designs (called Caf1-J3 and Caf1-J4) improved wound healing. Used together, they were generally better in wound healing than either design alone. Our findings suggest that short laminin-332 presented on Caf1 scaffolds can help with wound healing. The Caf1 system is easy to produce and can be customized. It offers potential as a new treatment for treating chronic wounds and inherited skin conditions.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© The Author(s) 2026.
